## Incident Report — 2024-07-30 STRRAT Infection

**Evidence reviewed:** `2024-07-30-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (11,562 frames, 585.7 s capture). No IDS/alert export or other artifacts were present alongside the pcap.

### Victim Host
| Field | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 | **172.16.1.66** | conversations, ARP |
| MAC | **00:1e:64:ec:f3:08** | ARP (`arp.src.proto_ipv4==172.16.1.66`) |
| Hostname | **DESKTOP-SKBR25F** | NBNS, LLMNR/mDNS, Kerberos, C2 beacon field |
| Logged-in user | **ccollier** | Kerberos `CNameString` (172.16.1.66 ↔ 172.16.1.4/DC), also confirmed inside the C2 beacon strings |

LAN: 172.16.1.0/24, gateway 172.16.1.1, domain controller `WIRESHARK-WS-DC` at 172.16.1.4, AD domain `wiresharkworkshop.online`.

### Malware Family
**STRRAT** (Java-based RAT/credential-stealer). **Signature-confirmed** — not inferred from behavior alone. The malware's C2 beacon protocol literally names itself in cleartext:

```
ping|STRRAT|1BE8292C|DESKTOP-SKBR25F|ccollier|Microsoft Windows 11 Pro|64-bit|Windows Defender|<base64 window title>|1.6|US:United States|Not Installed|<uptime>
```

TCP stream 83 (`172.16.1.66:49754 <-> 141.98.10.79:12132`) starts at t=76.99s and runs to the end of the capture (508.7 s duration), sending this "ping" heartbeat every ~5 seconds in plaintext, no TLS. Fields observed: bot ID `1BE8292C`, victim hostname/user, OS, installed AV (Windows Defender), STRRAT version `1.6`, geolocation `US:United States`, and base64-encoded active-window titles (decoded: "Home", "Documents", "Program Manager", and a PowerPoint window title), consistent with STRRAT's window-tracking/keylogging behavior.

Immediately before the beacon starts, three parallel TLS sessions to `repo1.maven.org` (199.232.196.209) transfer ~9 MB in under 6 seconds (t=64.8–70.7s), alongside a TLS session to `objects.githubusercontent.com` (185.199.110.133, ~828 KB, t=64.8–70.9s). This timing is consistent with the Java-based STRRAT payload pulling its JRE/dependency jars at launch, but the transfers are TLS-encrypted so the exact file(s) and any hash cannot be recovered from this capture. No plaintext file transfer was observed anywhere in the capture (`--export-objects http` yielded only `connecttest.txt` and an `ip-api.com` JSON response — both benign), so **no file name or SHA256 hash can be grounded in this evidence.**

### Indicators of Compromise

| Type | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| C2 endpoint | **141.98.10.79:12132** | TCP stream 83, plaintext `ping\|STRRAT\|...` beacon every ~5s for 508s, no DNS lookup preceded it (hardcoded IP in the malware config) |

No other IOCs (domains, URLs, file names/hashes) could be grounded strictly in the traffic. All other external endpoints observed (Microsoft/MSN/Office telemetry, Bing, Skype, WNS, `login.microsoftonline.com`, `github.com`/`objects.githubusercontent.com`, `repo1.maven.org`, `javadl-esd-secure.oracle.com`, `ip-api.com`) are legitimate services or self-geolocation lookups and are listed below as context, not indicators — `ip-api.com` (208.95.112.1) is worth flagging as a possible recon step (malware/scripts commonly call it to geolocate the victim, matching the `US:United States` field carried in the STRRAT beacon), but the request itself is to a legitimate public API and not inherently malicious.

**Benign/context traffic:** `wiresharkworkshop.online` AD domain traffic (LDAP/Kerberos/DCE-RPC/SMB to 172.16.1.4), Windows/Office/MSN/Bing/Skype/WNS telemetry, `client.wns.windows.com`, `oneclient.sfx.ms`, Oracle Java auto-update check (`javadl-esd-secure.oracle.com`), `github.com`/`objects.githubusercontent.com`, `repo1.maven.org` (Java package repo), `ip-api.com` geolocation lookup, SSDP/mDNS/LLMNR/NBNS local discovery.

### Summary
The Windows 11 workstation **DESKTOP-SKBR25F** (172.16.1.66, MAC 00:1e:64:ec:f3:08), logged in as domain user **ccollier**, is infected with **STRRAT**, confirmed by the malware's own self-identifying plaintext beacon protocol. The infected host maintained a persistent, unencrypted heartbeat channel to **141.98.10.79:12132** for over 8 minutes, reporting host fingerprint, security-software status, and active-window titles. The delivery mechanism could not be conclusively determined from this capture window: large TLS downloads from `repo1.maven.org` and `objects.githubusercontent.com` immediately precede the C2 beacon and are consistent with STRRAT's Java runtime/dependency staging, but the encrypted payload contents (and thus any file name or hash) are not recoverable from network evidence alone.
